title: Elara and the Time Echo
markdown:
The dusty lane behind Oakhaven Primary usually felt forgotten. Sunbeams thick with motes slanted between brick and overflowing bins. For Elara Meadowlight the lane was a map of footsteps: Mrs Gable’s clip-clop, always late for tea; Mr Fitzwilliam’s slow thoughtful tread; the Year Six football rumble that shook the shed. Today a new sound arrived, light and uneven, a shuffle as if someone were tiptoeing on cobwebs.

She had only meant to fetch a Frisbee heading for Mrs Higgins’s prize petunias. She froze. The shuffle did not belong. The lane looked fuzzy, as if seen through a smudged pane. The air tasted of static and old chalk. Near the rusty bike shed a figure rippled into place, tweed waistcoat a size too large, spectacles wobbly, and—Elara’s breath caught—see-through, pale as paper held to a window.

“Good afternoon,” the figure said, voice like rustling pages. “Are you the keeper of this time weirdness?”

“I’m Elara. I think I was getting my Frisbee.” She pointed at the petunias, which had gone oddly bright.

The figure adjusted see-through spectacles. “Elara Meadowlight. Sorcha Buttercup, Assistant Archivist of the Time Slip Department. You are caught in a stubborn time echo. Watch.”

The afternoon bell began, usually freedom, and came out wrong: flickering, notes blurred, too high, then too low, as if the bronze could not decide which year it belonged to.

This was the sort of afternoon Elara never meant to cause. She did not go looking for trouble. Trouble found her Frisbee. There had been the hamster, Mr Nibbles, freed because she thought he wanted air, and then the prize caterpillars, and then a classroom in silk. “It sounds like a frog in its throat,” she offered.

Sorcha sighed, pages turning. “Many frogs. Many timelines. This lane is caught between then and now. An inconvenient paperwork problem.”

They moved toward the bell. The air thickened, pre-storm buzzy. The chime cleared a fraction, and by the ancient oak stood another Sorcha, younger, solid enough to look anxious, tying shoelaces of ghostly string that would not hold.

“Excuse me,” Elara said. “Do you know why the bell is doing that?”

The younger one looked up. “Bell? What bell? I’m late for the filing seminar. Spectral forms will not file themselves.” She hurried off. Elara knew the footsteps at once: a flustered Sorcha. “She doesn’t know us. She’s younger. And she’s worried about forms.”

“The timeline is tangled,” Sorcha said. “We bump echoes of ourselves. Very inefficient. The cross-referencing alone.”

They retreated to the oak’s dappled shade. Sorcha paced, a faint rustle. Elara sat and drew patterns in the dust with a twig and let the lane be only lane for a minute: brick warmth, bin-shadow, a blackbird with no opinion about archives. A lorry passed on the far road and did not flicker. That, more than the ghost, made her trust the pause. A memory arrived that was not quite hers: a girl with bright ribbons, earnest, talking to a younger, more solid Sorcha by these same reaching branches.

“A promise,” Elara said. “It was about a promise.”

Sorcha froze mid-step. “What promise?”

“The girl promised you something. A time capsule. She’d hide it somewhere safe, for when you were ready. When you had finished all your filing.”

Sorcha’s brow creased, see-through. “A time capsule? My work is archival. Personal burying is not in the remit. Very unusual.”

Elara’s instincts tugged anyway. She walked the twisted roots, looking for old digging. The shimmer around the bell swelled. A wash of ghostly paperwork, notices and rules. An older Sorcha appeared, faint as worn paper, voice a dry rustle.

“Time messes need to be recorded. Untimely records are not good. Rule 7G, Section 4b.” She offered nothing else and blew away on an unseen wind.

“No help at all,” Elara said. Duty was one thing. This felt like a knot that wanted untying. “We have to find the capsule.”

A different echo came: not a step, a memory of one. A young girl giggling, digging with determined hands. Elara followed it with something deeper than ears and stopped by earth half-hidden in ivy. “Here.”

Sorcha’s hands went through soil as if it were mist and came back not with a box but a small carved wooden locket, warm even in ghostly fingers. Inside, on faded twilight velvet, a tiny scroll tied with silver thread.

To Sorcha, said the childish hand, ink still bright. When you feel you’ve finished all your filing, open this. I promise it will make you smile. From Rosie.

Sorcha held the locket and went a little more present, a warmer pale. The bell’s flicker stopped. One clear chime, true. The lane’s fuzzy edges sharpened. Damp earth. Sun-warmed brick. Oakhaven again.

She tucked the locket into the waistcoat with quiet respect, adjusted her spectacles, and for the first time Elara saw a smile try the see-through face.

“Very unusual,” Sorcha whispered, amused as an old chair creaking. “An incredibly well-filed memory. Excellent personal archive material.”

The lane was a lane: scuffs, stamps, a Frisbee at the petunia border where it had no right to look so ordinary. Elara picked it up. Mrs Gable’s clip-clop started up again, late for tea as ever, and did not echo twice. She had not meant to mend a timeline. She had meant to save Mrs Higgins’s flowers. The flowers were fine. The filing, for once, had a smile in it. She walked back toward the yard, listening for footsteps she knew, and left the oak to keep the rest.
characters: Elara Meadowlight (girl who never means to break rules but somehow does), Sorcha Buttercup (a local ghost who is mostly administrative)
audience: children aged 11-12, high-quality story for older children
